walkthroughs.body_html:
Ecosystems & Ecology — a core area of Environmental Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Ecosystems & Ecology brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Ecosystems & Ecology.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Typical energy transfer efficiency between trophic levels:
Why are tropical rainforest soils often nutrient-poor despite abundant vegetation?
options: Rainforests are deserts most of the year.
Rapid decomposition and uptake mean nutrients cycle quickly through living biomass, not soil.
They are larger than native species.
Rainforests have rich soils because they are productive.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between in-situ and ex-situ conservation?
options: One is for plants, the other for animals.
They are larger than native species.
They are alternative names for the same approach.
In-situ protects species in their natural habitat; ex-situ removes them to controlled settings like zoos or seed banks.

mcqs.q: Why are invasive species often more harmful than native species?
options: They are larger than native species.
They are inherently more aggressive than native species.
Rainforests are deserts most of the year.
They lack natural predators or competitors in their new environment, so they spread unchecked.
